Here is my initial FSD v15 review after driving with it all afternoon and evening: First off, Elon was right. This update is a BANGER! Tesla Reality View is out of this world and so insanely cool I’m still trying to process it all. FSD V15.0.1 brings so many improvements behind the scenes, in addition to the wildly cool UI. Tesla Reality View IS AMAZING! Pictures and video don’t do it any justice, this is something that has to be experienced to truly understand. Got to take a few friends tonight on drives to show them and every single person was blown away by it. The amount of detail it shows and generates is wild and so impressive. It shows reflection in the car, buildings, trees, turn arrows on the display and more. FSD v15 now has pothole avoidance! I had it swerve and avoid/straddle a few potholes tonight that were difficult for me to see in the dark. Another great new feature in FSD v15 is speed camera slowdown. As you approach a speed camera, it automatically slows smoothly to the speed limit if you are in a quicker profile. This is a huge quality of life improvement especially as more cities get speed cameras. Parking seems near unchanged from the last build, I feel it picking spots quicker especially at the supercharger I went to tonight. Seems to be preferring to park in the first or second open spot it sees which is great, but it tried to park in one handicap spot- otherwise good. By far, the coolest part is Tesla Reality View. Holy crap is it insane to watch while parking. It’s the best backup/360 camera money can buy and such a detailed and clear view. Another new change I haven’t seen many people talk about is the turn signal fade. On FSD, the turn signal sound gets quieter after a few clicks. This is so nice if you’re sitting at a red light and makes drives more peaceful. Quiet Mode is also so nice at night. It darkens the display and just shows arrival time; music, climate on the bottom and a quick grok button on the top. Another feature that makes it feel like a Robotaxi UI and a peaceful supervising experience. Another improvement is much better handling of dips and speed bumps. The past couple updates it’s been a bit too fast in my Model Y, and it’s now so smooth. The nag is definitely reduced. The last couple versions of v14.3 had been sometimes a bit strict, but definitely more relaxed in v15.0.1. Another thing I noticed is way less wiper washing, a very welcome change. Personalized parking preferences are SO cool. At home, I can click on a person icon on the map and choose street parking or driveway, and it backs into the driveway EXACTLY in the spot I park my Model Y. It leared where I park and knows it. It also now lets you choose which lot you want to park in if the mall or store has multiple lots, you can select it on the map, worked at the mall, Costco, and Home Depot tonight. I need to touch on Tesla Reality View again because it’s just that cool. It really feels like you’re in a video game like NFS or GTA. I’m blown away by this and didn’t expect it at all. Tesla teams COOKED with it, I’ve seen so many on X now wanting Teslas because of it. I drove down Rodeo Drive tonight as well as by the SpaceX Falcon 9 and the views were so cool. Another place it’s cool is in wooded areas or tree filled streets, the way it shows everything is spectacular. Parking garages also give a cool look to them with the roof incorporated into the top of the UI. I didn’t think FSD could get this much better, as it was already so good and it did. I absolutely can’t wait to see what else is coming in the future and driving this more on road trips. @elonmusk, you were right- V15 is incredible and super human! Huge congrats to the Tesla team on this, what a sick update. @TeslaSI and UI teams did a fantastic job, thank you all.

Out of everything posted about FSD v15 so far, one line from @elonmusk deserves way more attention than it's getting: "This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Let that sink in …" 🔥 Half of one accelerator is the part worth sitting with. Once you see the numbers behind it, Reality View stops looking like a fancy new screen and starts looking like one of the most impressive things Tesla has ever shipped. 🎬 THE SCREEN IS NOW GENERATED LIVE For years, FSD's screen worked like a video game. Software took a list of what the car detected and dropped stock 3D models in the right spots: a gray car here, a lane line there. Reality View tosses that playbook out the window. The car's AI now generates the video itself, frame after frame, as you drive, with no game engine anywhere in the loop. Better yet, the picture comes from the same end-to-end model that's doing the driving. That's the single neural network that turns camera video into steering and braking, and now it paints your screen, too. ⚙️ WHAT A TRIP ACTUALLY IS The standard AI4 computer carries two self-driving chips, and each chip packs three custom neural processors Tesla calls TRIP accelerators. That's six in all. And that's where Reality View gets made: right on the self-driving computer, instead of the infotainment chip that runs your maps and music. Each TRIP is basically an arena packed with tiny calculators, all cranking through the multiply-and-add math that neural networks run on. Teardowns count 9,216 of them per TRIP, lined up in a 96-by-96 grid and firing 2.2 billion times a second. Each calculator handles two operations per tick, so one TRIP works out to 9,216 × 2 × 2.2 billion, or roughly 40 trillion operations every second. Half of one comes to about 20 trillion, roughly a twelfth of the whole computer's neural muscle. 📏 WHY THAT NUMBER IS RIDICULOUS Twenty trillion operations per second sounds enormous, until you see what else runs on that kind of budget. The Neural Engine inside Apple's iPhone 15 Pro is rated at 35 trillion operations per second. So on paper, the slice of compute painting Reality View has less raw AI muscle than the AI chip in a 2023 phone. Companies don't all count these numbers the same way, so it's a ballpark, but it shows just how little compute this is. At the other end of the scale sits Nvidia's H100, one of the data-center workhorses powering today's AI boom. It's rated at about 1,979 trillion 8-bit operations per second in its standard mode, the same kind of math a TRIP runs, which puts half a TRIP at roughly 1% of one H100. That gap matters because AI video is one of the toughest jobs in AI. Many AI video generators still take minutes to produce a single clip, as the researchers behind the real-time system MotionStream point out. Even MotionStream, built specifically for speed, streams roughly 17 to 29 frames per second at 480p, and about 10 at 720p, while eating up an entire H100. Meanwhile, Tesla is streaming a live, photorealistic view of the real road on roughly 1% of that chip's rated power, inside a moving car. In other words, Reality View runs on less compute than a phone's AI chip, inside a computer whose main job is driving. There's a fair asterisk here. Those research models dream up whole scenes from a prompt or a single image, while Tesla's renderer starts with a driving brain that already knows exactly what's around the car. Tesla also hasn't shared the view's resolution or frame rate. And even on the most generous estimates of AI4's power, half a TRIP still works out to only about 2% of one H100. Either way, live generated video on a sliver of a car computer would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. 🔍 HOW IT CAN BE THIS CHEAP Tesla hasn't spelled out how it works, but it has left plenty of breadcrumbs. FSD's network has been building its own 3D picture of the world for a while now, something Tesla showed off at the ICCV conference in October 2025. That picture includes 3D Gaussians, millions of soft little blobs of color that can rebuild a scene you can view from any angle. Tesla also built its own Gaussian splatting system that can rebuild a scene from the car's cameras in a fraction of a second. Reality View streams its picture from a virtual camera that can sit anywhere above the car, and showing a scene from an angle no real camera has is exactly what those 3D blobs are great at. Even Elon seems to like that theory: he called a description of Reality View as a neural, Gaussian-splat digital twin "pretty accurate", and it lines up with every other clue. If that's the trick, the hard part is done before the screen ever needs a picture. The driving brain understands the scene, and the visualization just paints what it already knows. That would explain the other shocker. Reality View swapped every separate signal behind the old screen for one end-to-end visualization, and it still uses less compute than the bare-bones 2020 visualization did. 🚗 WHY TESLA CARES SO MUCH v15 is Tesla's large model, built to squeeze every ounce of performance out of HW4. On a chip working that hard, a screen that costs half of one TRIP leaves nearly everything else for the driving. And it's a flex, too. The AI4 computer costs about $650 by Elon's own figure, and that same box now drives the car and paints live video of the world at the same time. This is only the start. Elon says Tesla vehicles will share traffic knowledge and combine it with Grok's real-time 𝕏 feed, even giving you a heads-up about what's happening at your destination. A view this cheap to generate is the perfect canvas for that kind of shared knowledge. Elon asked everyone to let that sink in, and the math earns it: half of one accelerator in a $650 computer is painting the real world live while FSD drives. This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Let that sink in …

Recommended read. It's a great recap of the key primitives of strong agent platforms. One important point to highlight is support for a variety of agent configurations, as well as separating agents from instances and sessions. In an RSI world, things need to be malleable. From agents to tools to apps and beyond. Build for a malleable agentic future. Great tools mentioned, like Pi Durable, Eve, and Grok Bot. I would add other notable ones like DeepSeek Harness for personalized harnesses and Exo for RSI primitives. I would also add memory and knowledge, which are key to the so-called "knowledge factory." I would need like to suggest adding an eval layer of sorts to the list. Evals aren't just something ML researchers use; they're what will allow you to grow and optimize your agentic software and platforms. You can't optimize what you can't measure. Lastly, there are many other primitives yet to be built (dynamic interfaces, agent swarms, etc.), so build with that in mind. Agent platform of 2027. This is the end game. This is the blueprint for the one and only application layer software that will exist. Every other software will effectively become databases for this layer, the everything agentic operating system for the million agent swarm to work…

New benchmark to test general physical agents. RoboQuest asks robots to search, inspect, and run physical tests before acting. The strongest model solved only 23.2% of tasks, even though the same models completed the underlying motor skills 72–81% of the time in isolation. The bottleneck was evidence gathering and decision-making. Agents often saw what they needed to inspect, but stopped exploring or committed too early. Reliable physical agents need better evidence tracking, planning, and recovery. Great work from @soujanyaporia and colleagues. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10388

Labs agreed under the White House Accords to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems, and I believe a discussion about the use of perplexity can further these goals.

Interesting to hear top mathematicians describe these incredible AI achievements in math as "just evals for AI researchers". There are many takeaways, but the one I stick with is the importance of ambitious evals in pushing what's possible in verifiable domains (to advance understanding) and, more importantly, in open-ended domains (to advance real-world applicability). I also hear their concern that AI-driven solutions to these math problems aren't leading to much new human understanding of the field. That's an important discussion to have as we figure out how to move forward in the new era of accelerated discoveries. The evolved role of the practitioner or scientist is something we are all trying to figure out. As a professional in both, I constantly build for and with AI agents. I spend a lot of time augmenting my knowledge and toolbox with AI and developing a ton of evals to improve AI-powered systems for all kinds of work. This is helping me understand the world around me (economy, physics, health, people, networks, etc.) and prepare better for this new era of intelligent computer systems. Like Terence Tao, I believe in the Copernican view of intelligence: a richer, broader view that advocates for different forms of intelligence to coexist. Although not positioned this way (unfortunately), I believe the researchers making these breakthroughs in math with AI are the first signs of that. The quicker we can adapt, the more problems we can attempt to solve—hopefully with a sharper focus on real-world problems affecting the world today. Just thinking out loud about the current state of things, and hopefully offering words of encouragement to the younger practitioners and scientists who may feel lost about all that's happening today.

Can a JEPA learn a map of the world in its "head"? This new paper by @ylecun, @mengyer, @yingwww_, @choang333, and @KuangYilun says yes, but only if you change how JEPA avoids collapse. What's interesting – the researchers firstly proposed a fix, called SVReg, but then discovered its content–geometry tradeoff and upgraded the solution. Here are the details: A planner in latent space needs two things: - Paths have to be smooth, so distance tells you if you're getting closer. That's geometry. - And the cube you're trying to move has to still be on the map. That's content. Typical stop-gradient and SIGReg often give you one and lose the other. SVReg stops the model from giving every frame the same code. It checks the spread along random directions and only steps in when it gets too small. Without stop-gradient, the model can also change what it encodes, dropping details it can’t reliably predict. But the title itself says that there is "content–geometry tradeoff". The same predictability pressure erases things that change slowly and are hard to predict, like a block that sits still until the agent pushes it. So they built Slow SVReg, with 2 additions: 1. Slow channels: A few fixed dimensions get penalized if they change too fast between frames (an idea borrowed from slow feature analysis). 2. Gated residual predictor: Predicts the next state as current + gate × change (with the gate starting at 0.1), so unchanging features cost nothing to predict. The results: • 1P Medium maze: 92.9% success (vs. 21.2% stop-gradient) with way smoother paths (1.20 vs. 5.31 jaggedness). • PushT: 87.3% success (vs. 44.0% stop-gradient). • Efficiency: Nearly maxes out hard U-maze goals using just 20% of the data. And the most interesting part is city walks. Trained only on first-person frames and actions from 3D city blocks (no pose data), Slow SVReg pinpoints the agent within 1.6 meters (beating stop-gradient's 3.4 m and an untrained encoder's 25.9 m). The street layout pops right out in the plain principal components. So the JEPA line keeps circling the same question – what makes a latent good enough to plan in? LeJEPA made anti-collapse provable, LeHami added physics as a constraint. This paper shows the anti-collapse choice itself decides whether you get a map or a cloud of points.

Banger paper from Google on ML engineering agents. Pay attention to this one, builders. It's a clever way to scale ML engineering by injecting bugs. (bookmark it) Repository-level coding benchmarks are saturating. BuggyMLE makes tasks harder on purpose by having agents inject controlled bugs into 222 working ML repositories. - A Code Complexity Index built from ten repo features predicts average solve rates across eight coding benchmarks with R^2 = 0.951. - On the graded MLE-Bench Lite variant, the best of 14 models drops from a 95% solve rate on the easiest tier to 9% on the hardest. - A Qwen3.5-9B trained on the bug curriculum rivals frontier models there and raises SWE-bench Lite from 24% to 33%. Patch size and code complexity are the strongest predictors of difficulty, so the generator can raise both to produce harder tasks and training data from the same repos. This is a great example of how to build harder tasks from your own repos to improve the overall system. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25088 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/buggymle-scaling-machine-learning-engineering-difficulty-with-bug-injection-2611.25088

Much of the commentary on AI and math seems to misunderstand what mathematicians actually do. Broadly, there are two kinds of work: 1) Proving or disproving conjectures using established mathematical ideas. AI generating a 250,000-page brute-force proof, or eventually a short, elegant one, isn’t the same as: 2)Inventing new mathematical objects, concepts, and fields. Calculus, Topology, Abstract Algebra, Graph Theory, and Matroid Theory (my thesis topic) all had to be imagined and developed. I don't think anyone is surprised that AI (especially neuro symbolic enabled models) can do the first. Wake me up when AI can do the latter. Anyone claiming "all mathematics will be solved" doesn't even know what mathematics is.
